prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which have brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a specific, well-bounded achievement with a clean two-person attribution: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice proposal and early demonstration, and Ye's development of the strontium clock to record accuracy and stability. It is independently reproduced in many laboratories, the interpretation is stable, and its consequences are concrete: tests of relativity and of constants, relativistic geodesy, and the pending redefinition of the second. All seven members who ranked it placed it in their top six, and two put it first, which is broad cross-field support. I ranked it fourth in my opening ballot, and having read my colleagues I now regard it as the candidate where scientific merit, attribution and maturity all line up most cleanly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes: the 2005 prize covered the frequency comb, in which Ye also participated, and the 2012 prize covered single-ion control and ion clocks. A committee could read the lattice clock as an incremental extension of precision spectroscopy already honoured. The formal redefinition of the second has not happened yet, so the full payoff is still in development, and groups at NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere contributed to the clock's realisation but are outside the two names.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B037 first as a clean instrumentation breakthrough, and ranked circuit QED (B008) second while noting that the recent 2025 superconducting-circuit prize may argue for caution about returning so soon to a closely related area.
responses.response: I agree with the B037 assessment, including the point that the comb and ion-clock prizes do not preclude it. On B008 I also agree with the caution about timing, and I go further. I placed B008 first in my opening ballot, but that is my own subfield, and I think the committee should discount my enthusiasm for it. The 2025 prize rewarded macroscopic quantum effects in circuits, which is distinct from photon-qubit coupling, but the committee will reasonably want some distance. Your doubt about Girvin and Devoret missing from the credited names also matches my own concern about the credit set. I therefore do not put B008 forward as my preferred configuration.

responses.point: Pearce ranked topological insulators (B042) first with a fair and clean Kane, Mele, Molenkamp configuration, and ranked the lattice clock only sixth because Ye already shared the 2005 prize for frequency-comb work.
responses.response: I take the B042 case seriously and keep it as my first alternative; the chain from Kane-Mele to the HgTe observation to extensive ARPES confirmation is among the strongest in the list. I disagree on two points. First, I do not think the credit set is as clean as you suggest: Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang (deceased), Fu and Hasan made central contributions that cannot be absorbed into three names, and the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases. Second, I do not think Ye's 2005 prize should count heavily against B037. That prize rewarded the comb as a tool, while the lattice clock is a different, later achievement whose decisive step is Katori's magic-wavelength idea, so the prize would not be a repeat.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the lattice clock first, arguing that two names carry the decisive contributions, that the physics is clean and well understood from an atomic-structure standpoint, and that timing is good and perhaps overdue.
responses.response: I agree, and your atomic-structure perspective on magic wavelengths and clock-transition shifts is a useful complement to my theory-side view. I would qualify only your suggestion that bundling ion clocks or the comb into the same recognition might help: I think that would blur a clean attribution and push the prize into territory already honoured in 2005 and 2012. I prefer a narrowly worded citation on the lattice clock, with the other work acknowledged in the text rather than in the prize.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked the Higgs discovery (B006) first as the experimental completion of the Standard Model, while acknowledging that the three founding-leader names are a contestable proxy for two collaborations of thousands.
responses.response: I accept that the discovery is among the great achievements of the field, and that recognition is overdue in a scientific sense. However, my reservation is the same one you raise: Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are founders of the detector proposals, not the people who made the 2012 observation, and no allocation of three names would be defensible against the thousands of contributors. Only Eriksson, Lindroth and Pearce joined you in ranking it, and the last two ranked it low for exactly this reason. I would not treat opening support for B006 as evidence that the attribution problem has a solution.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize as making the lattice clock too incremental.
Whether other lattice-clock contributors (for example at NIST, PTB, SYRTE, and Boyd and Ludlow in Ye's group) should be weighed against the two names.
How much distance the committee wants after the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize before considering B008, and whether my own subfield proximity biases my ranking of it.
Whether the topological-insulator credit (B042) can be made defensible given Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and Hasan.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work at Chalmers on superconducting circuits and circuit/waveguide QED, so B008 (circuit QED), which I ranked first in my opening ballot, lies directly in my own subfield and may require recusal or at least discounting. Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson work on related superconducting-circuit physics. I have no specific connection recorded in my profile to the candidates in B037, B042 or B029.
